title: Shortest Alternating Color Paths
description:
# Shortest Alternating Color Paths

You are given a directed graph with `n` nodes labeled from `0` to `n - 1`. Each directed edge is colored red or blue. Return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the length of the shortest path from node `0` to node `i` whose edge colors strictly alternate. If node `i` cannot be reached by such a path, set `answer[i]` to `-1`.

The first edge may have either color; consecutive edges must then have different colors. Length counts edges, and the distance to node `0` itself is `0`. An entry `[u,v]` in `redEdges` or `blueEdges` is a directed edge from `u` to `v` of that color.

## Example 1:

**Input:** n = 3, redEdges = [[0,1],[1,2]], blueEdges = []
**Output:** [0,1,-1]
**Explanation:** Node `1` is reachable by one red edge. Node `2` would require two red edges in a row, so it is not reachable by an alternating path.

## Example 2:

**Input:** n = 3, redEdges = [[0,1]], blueEdges = [[1,2]]
**Output:** [0,1,2]
**Explanation:** The path `0 -> 1 -> 2` uses red then blue.

## Constraints:

*   `1 <= n <= 100`
*   `0 <= redEdges.length, blueEdges.length <= 400`
*   `redEdges[i].length == blueEdges[i].length == 2`
*   `0 <= from, to < n` for every edge `[from, to]`.
*   Parallel edges and self-loops may appear.

tests.description: Edges pointing back toward zero do not make later nodes reachable.
The shortest numeric path is invalid when two consecutive blue edges would be needed.
Self-loops and parallel colored edges must not break alternating BFS.
Node 1 must be reachable in both color states; node-only visited sets miss nodes 2 and 3.
Starting with the blue edge gives a shorter route to node 2.
Cycles should not cause infinite traversal, and same-color exits remain blocked.
A longer chain alternates across disconnected-looking red and blue layers.
Parallel edges should not change the answer or enqueue the same state repeatedly.
Reachability can improve after revisiting a node through the opposite last-edge color.

solutions.name: BFS With Last Color State
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build two adjacency lists, one for red edges and one for blue edges. Run BFS over states `(node, lastColor)`, where `lastColor` is the color of the edge used to enter the node. From that state, only edges of the opposite color can be used next. Initialize node `0` in both last-color states so the first real edge may be red or blue.

## Key Insight

The shortest-path unit is not just the node. Arriving at the same node after a red edge and after a blue edge gives different legal next moves, so the visited and distance arrays must include the last-edge color.

## Complexity Analysis

Each color-state is visited at most once and each colored edge is scanned from the opposite-color state. Time Complexity: O(n + r + b). Space Complexity: O(n + r + b).
solutions.code: import java.util.*; class Solution { public int[] shortestAlternatingPaths(int n, int[][] redEdges, int[][] blueEdges) { List<Integer>[][] graph = new ArrayList[2][n]; for (int color = 0; color < 2; color++) { for (int node = 0; node < n; node++) { graph[color][node] = new ArrayList<>(); } } for (int[] edge : redEdges) { graph[0][edge[0]].add(edge[1]); } for (int[] edge : blueEdges) { graph[1][edge[0]].add(edge[1]); } int[][] distance = new int[2][n]; Arrays.fill(distance[0], -1); Arrays.fill(distance[1], -1); ArrayDeque<int[]> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(); queue.offer(new int[]{0, 0}); queue.offer(new int[]{0, 1}); distance[0][0] = 0; distance[1][0] = 0; while (!queue.isEmpty()) { int[] state = queue.poll(); int node = state[0]; int lastColor = state[1]; int nextColor = 1 - lastColor; for (int next : graph[nextColor][node]) { if (distance[nextColor][next] == -1) { distance[nextColor][next] = distance[lastColor][node] + 1; queue.offer(new int[]{next, nextColor}); } } } int[] answer = new int[n]; for (int node = 0; node < n; node++) { if (distance[0][node] == -1) { answer[node] = distance[1][node]; } else if (distance[1][node] == -1) { answer[node] = distance[0][node]; } else { answer[node] = Math.min(distance[0][node], distance[1][node]); } } return answer; } }

solutions.name: Layered Graph BFS
solutions.description:
## Approach

Duplicate the graph into two layers: one layer represents states where the last edge was red, and the other represents states where the last edge was blue. A red edge from `u` to `v` becomes an edge from the blue-last state of `u` to the red-last state of `v`; blue edges are converted symmetrically. Then run an ordinary BFS on the expanded graph.

## Key Insight

Alternation can be encoded into the graph topology. Once each state already remembers the last edge color, a valid alternating path is just a normal path in the expanded graph.

## Complexity Analysis

The expanded graph has `2n` states and one expanded edge for every original colored edge. Time Complexity: O(n + r + b). Space Complexity: O(n + r + b).
solutions.code: import java.util.*; class Solution { public int[] shortestAlternatingPaths(int n, int[][] redEdges, int[][] blueEdges) { List<Integer>[] expanded = new ArrayList[2 * n]; for (int i = 0; i < expanded.length; i++) { expanded[i] = new ArrayList<>(); } for (int[] edge : redEdges) { expanded[n + edge[0]].add(edge[1]); } for (int[] edge : blueEdges) { expanded[edge[0]].add(n + edge[1]); } int[] distance = new int[2 * n]; Arrays.fill(distance, -1); ArrayDeque<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>(); queue.offer(0); queue.offer(n); distance[0] = 0; distance[n] = 0; while (!queue.isEmpty()) { int state = queue.poll(); for (int next : expanded[state]) { if (distance[next] == -1) { distance[next] = distance[state] + 1; queue.offer(next); } } } int[] answer = new int[n]; for (int node = 0; node < n; node++) { int redLast = distance[node]; int blueLast = distance[n + node]; if (redLast == -1) { answer[node] = blueLast; } else if (blueLast == -1) { answer[node] = redLast; } else { answer[node] = Math.min(redLast, blueLast); } } return answer; } }

solutions.name: Dijkstra On Color State Graph
solutions.description:
## Approach

Model each state as `(node, lastColor)` and add every colored edge as a transition that is legal only from the opposite last color. Because all transitions have weight `1`, BFS is faster, but a priority queue Dijkstra implementation demonstrates the general shortest-path version of the same state graph.

## Key Insight

The color rule is a state constraint, not a post-processing filter. Once the state includes the last color, standard shortest-path machinery can be applied directly.

## Complexity Analysis

There are `2n` states and `r + b` transitions. With a priority queue, Time Complexity: O((n + r + b) log n). Space Complexity: O(n + r + b).
solutions.code: import java.util.*; class Solution { public int[] shortestAlternatingPaths(int n, int[][] redEdges, int[][] blueEdges) { List<int[]>[] graph = new ArrayList[n]; for (int node = 0; node < n; node++) { graph[node] = new ArrayList<>(); } for (int[] edge : redEdges) { graph[edge[0]].add(new int[]{edge[1], 0}); } for (int[] edge : blueEdges) { graph[edge[0]].add(new int[]{edge[1], 1}); } int inf = 1_000_000; int[][] dist = new int[2][n]; Arrays.fill(dist[0], inf); Arrays.fill(dist[1], inf); PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingInt(a -> a[0])); dist[0][0] = 0; dist[1][0] = 0; pq.offer(new int[]{0, 0, 0}); pq.offer(new int[]{0, 0, 1}); while (!pq.isEmpty()) { int[] state = pq.poll(); int currentDist = state[0]; int node = state[1]; int lastColor = state[2]; if (currentDist != dist[lastColor][node]) { continue; } for (int[] edge : graph[node]) { int next = edge[0]; int color = edge[1]; if (color == lastColor) { continue; } if (currentDist + 1 < dist[color][next]) { dist[color][next] = currentDist + 1; pq.offer(new int[]{dist[color][next], next, color}); } } } int[] answer = new int[n]; for (int node = 0; node < n; node++) { int best = Math.min(dist[0][node], dist[1][node]); answer[node] = best >= inf ? -1 : best; } return answer; } }

solutions.name: State Relaxation Bellman-Ford
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep two distance arrays: `dist[0][v]` is the best distance to `v` ending with a red edge, and `dist[1][v]` is the best distance ending with a blue edge. Repeatedly relax every red edge from the previous blue layer and every blue edge from the previous red layer until no value changes.

## Key Insight

This is the same two-layer state graph as the BFS solutions, expressed as edge relaxation. It is slower, but useful for seeing exactly which color-state transitions are legal.

## Complexity Analysis

At most `2n` improving edge counts are relevant before all shortest alternating paths stabilize. Time Complexity: O(n * (r + b)). Space Complexity: O(n).
solutions.code: import java.util.*; class Solution { public int[] shortestAlternatingPaths(int n, int[][] redEdges, int[][] blueEdges) { int inf = 1_000_000; int[][] dist = new int[2][n]; Arrays.fill(dist[0], inf); Arrays.fill(dist[1], inf); dist[0][0] = 0; dist[1][0] = 0; for (int pass = 0; pass < 2 * n; pass++) { boolean changed = false; int[][] next = new int[2][n]; next[0] = dist[0].clone(); next[1] = dist[1].clone(); for (int[] edge : redEdges) { if (dist[1][edge[0]] + 1 < next[0][edge[1]]) { next[0][edge[1]] = dist[1][edge[0]] + 1; changed = true; } } for (int[] edge : blueEdges) { if (dist[0][edge[0]] + 1 < next[1][edge[1]]) { next[1][edge[1]] = dist[0][edge[0]] + 1; changed = true; } } dist = next; if (!changed) { break; } } int[] answer = new int[n]; for (int node = 0; node < n; node++) { int best = Math.min(dist[0][node], dist[1][node]); answer[node] = best >= inf ? -1 : best; } return answer; } }
